items.title: Find your PCA match time
items.detail: Qualifying runs Nov 30–Dec 4. Check when you play and when to sign in.

items.title: Choose Japan dates after PCA
items.detail: Check your PCA schedule and return flight before booking Tokyo.

items.title: PCA Open · men’s singles
items.detail: Final entries are posted. Confirm your match and sign-in times with PCA.

items.title: Step in on the short high ball
items.detail: In Tennis Training → My game, try the ten-ball set. Take the ball on the rise and count how many land deep down the line.

items.title: Watch juniors at Rizal Memorial
items.detail: Start with a morning session. Check the order of play and ask about spectator entry.

items.title: Rizal Memorial · second J30
items.detail: Same hard courts. Qualifying starts Sun Nov 29.

items.title: PCA Open · main draw
items.detail: Keep Japan flexible if you advance.

items.title: Get used to the heat
items.detail: Start with easy time outside and short hits. Build up gradually and take cooling breaks.

items.title: F45 · BGC Stopover
items.detail: Optional coached group strength and cardio classes.

items.title: Rizal Memorial · public courts
items.detail: Open the PSC portal, choose Rizal Memorial Tennis Hall and check available slots.

photos.caption: Rizal Memorial Sports Complex from above

items.title: ProServe · Santa Ana
items.detail: Indoor backup. Choose the Santa Ana location, Tennis, then an available slot.

items.title: Grab
items.detail: Uber for Manila. A U.S. Chase Sapphire Visa worked for rides.

items.title: Move It
items.detail: Motorcycle taxi. Check pickup, fare and payment in the app.

items.title: GCash
items.detail: Cash to a friend worked for getting balance and pesos. Send enough for a few days if using BofA. A repeat transfer was blocked for three days in one case.

items.title: Pesos + Visa
items.detail: Carry small peso notes for cash-only spots. U.S. Visa worked where cards are accepted. Walk for nearby stops and open the phone for the ride or map.

items.title: Manila Polo Club
items.detail: Private club. Arrange a guest visit with JR. Upscale setting. You preferred PCA’s courts.
items.meta: About 9 km · 25–45 min by moto · Been

Manila Polo Club from the grounds

items.title: Kerry Sports · BGC
items.detail: JR is listed as a coach at the Shangri-La. Ask him about guest access.

items.detail: JR heads the varsity program. Ask which courts the team is using.
items.meta: About 2.5 km to campus · 10–15 min by moto

items.detail: Covered clay. You already hit here with JR.
items.meta: About 3 km · 10–20 min by moto · Been

items.title: Rockwell
items.detail: JR mentioned Rockwell. His current coaching location there still needs confirmation.

items.title: Robinsons Manila · supermarket
items.detail: The supermarket and French Baker are on Level 1 in the Adriatico Wing.

items.title: Malate Koreatown
items.detail: Korean neighborhood around Remedios and Adriatico. Try samgyeopsal or Korean-Chinese jjajangmyeon. Allow ₱500–900 for K-BBQ.

items.title: Wai Ying · Binondo lunch
items.detail: Order roast duck rice or congee. Add hakaw if you’re sharing.

photos.caption: Wai Ying in the Binondo neighborhood guide

items.title: Quiapo · Muslim Town
items.detail: Go around the Golden Mosque for Filipino-Muslim food. Try pastil, rice topped with shredded meat. Allow ₱100–250 for snacks and a rice meal.

photos.caption: Another view of the Golden Mosque

items.title: BGC · High Street
items.detail: Walkable modern Manila: public art, shopping and air-conditioned breaks. Go for the walk. Allow ₱500–1,000 if you sit down for dinner.

items.title: Intramuros · Fort Santiago
items.detail: Go for the walls, old Manila and the river. Easy to pair with Baywalk.

photos.caption: Fort Santiago inside the walled city

items.title: The Aristocrat · Malate
items.detail: Good, close and open late. Easy dinner near Alpha Grandview.

items.title: Manila Polo Club
items.detail: Upscale club. You liked PCA’s courts better.

photos.caption: Covered tennis courts at Manila Polo Club

items.title: Mendokoro Ramenba
items.detail: You had tsukemen, the dipping ramen. Pretty good. Multiple branches.

items.title: Bikram Yoga Manila
items.detail: You went to hot yoga. Keep it easy near match days.

items.title: Binondo · Chinatown
items.detail: Chinese-Filipino food crawl. Split fresh lumpia at New Po-Heng, fried chicken at Sincerity and hopia from Eng Bee Tin. Budget ₱350–600.

photos.caption: Binondo Church, near the start of Ongpin

items.title: Manila Baywalk
items.detail: Closest sunset. Walk the waterfront. Dolomite Beach is for looking, with no swim access.

items.title: Anilao · Batangas
items.detail: Optional full day for reef snorkeling or diving. Skip it if you want to stay near the courts.

items.title: Fortune Island · Nasugbu
items.detail: Boat trip for the cliffs and hilltop ruins. Confirm crossings and weather.
items.meta: About 90 km to Nasugbu · 2½–4 hr by car + boat

items.title: Subic Bay
items.detail: Beach and forest in one trip. Good overnight if you want both.

items.title: Hinulugang Taktak · Antipolo

items.title: Yu Kimura · KIMRA
items.detail: Spent over a decade at UNDERCOVER, including menswear and accessories production. KIMRA’s debut drew on 1990s European hardcore techno and included a cap with a neck shade and removable sweatband. Ask through KIMRA’s form about how that accessory reached its first sample.
items.draft: Hi Kimura-san, I’m Tom Oh from LA. I saw the KIMRA cap with the neck shade and removable sweatband. I’m making a tennis bandana and working out how it should feel after an hour on court. Would you have time for a short coffee in Tokyo to talk about what you test on a first sample?

items.title: Takayuki Fujii · nonnative

items.title: Tetsuya Nagato · UNDERCOVER PRODUCTION
items.detail: @tetsuyanagato · Co-directed UNDERCOVER’s 35th-anniversary behind-the-scenes film. Follow how he turns studio work and fittings into a story. Start with the Tokyo chapter of but beautiful 4… and ask how he chooses what to show from the making process.
items.draft: Hi Nagato-san, I’m Tom from LA. In the Tokyo chapter of but beautiful 4…, I liked seeing the work at the atelier before the looks went to Paris. I’m documenting my own first samples. How do you decide which parts of the process are worth showing?

items.title: VERDY · Graphic artist

items.title: NIGO · NOWHERE and HUMAN MADE

items.title: Tetsu Nishiyama · WTAPS

I’m working through the same problem on a much smaller scale with a tennis bandana. Would you have time for a quick coffee in Tokyo to talk about how you decide what to carry over from the artwork?

items.title: Behind the scenes at a joint running-apparel exhibition, with an honest talk by the MMA, Ranor and RYOGEN directors ([VLOG] ランニングアパレルブランド合同展示会に密着。MMA、Ranor、RYOGENブランドディレクターの本音トーク！)
items.detail: Japan's indie running brands (MMA, Ranor, RYOGEN) all make in Japan, show to wholesale buyers at small joint exhibitions in Tokyo, and say a brand survives on delivering the numbers, not on taste. Why: It shows Tom how a one-person Tokyo apparel brand actually runs (B2B exhibitions four times a year, Japanese factories, short lead times, cash-flow pressure), and the directors openly want more young brands and overseas buyers to come to their shows, which is an opening for a tennis/running bandana maker. Contact: Yuichi Shibui (MMA founder), IG @shibuinsta_mania https://www.instagram.com/shibuinsta_mania/ and MMA @mountainmartialarts https://www.instagram.com/mountainmartialarts/ ; Ranor (made-in-Japan running wear), IG @ranor9378 https://www.instagram.com/ranor9378/ , www.ranor.jp ; RYOGEN, IG @ryogen.jp https://www.instagram.com/ryogen.jp/

items.title: "[INTRODUCTION] Mountain Martial Arts, obsessed with design and function. But when did it start, and who started it? The brand's origin, product details and history, introduced again ([INTRODUCTION] デザインと機能にこだわったマウンテンマーシャルアーツ。でも、いつから、誰が始めたの？ブランドスタートのきっかけから商品のこだわり、歴史まであらためてご紹介！)"
items.detail: Yuichi Shibui is a graphic designer and avid runner, not a trained clothing designer, who built a one-person, all made-in-Japan running brand by mixing vintage and street taste with top technical fabrics, which is close to what Tom is trying to do with tennis. Why: Shibui is the clearest model in Tokyo for a sport-first apparel brand run by one person with Japanese factories, and he says he got his first big collaboration (Joe Grant) because someone noticed the product on a run. Tom can open with running and his bandanas, and ask about Japanese factories, minimums and Polartec-style fabric access. Contact: Yuichi Shibui (MMA founder and director), Instagram @shibuinsta_mania https://www.instagram.com/shibuinsta_mania/ ; brand Instagram @mountainmartialarts https://www.instagram.com/mountainmartialarts/ ; web store https://store.mountainmartialarts.tokyo/

items.title: "TOKYO GUERRILLA RUN: a new running community in Tokyo, MOUNTAIN MARTIAL ARTS x Tani wa Hashiru. Why are they starting guerrilla runs in Tokyo? (【TOKYO GUERRILLA RUN /東京ゲリララン】東京に新たなランニングコミュニティ/MOUNTAIN MARTIAL ARTS ×タニは走る。/彼らはなぜ東京でゲリラランを始めるのか？！)"
items.detail: MMA's Tokyo Guerrilla Runs are free, unannounced night runs posted only in disappearing Instagram Stories, and Shibui explicitly wants foreign runners to join, so showing up to one is Tom's easiest way to meet him. Why: Tom runs, and this is a low-pressure way to spend an hour with Shibui and his running crowd before talking about bandanas or making. Watching MMA's and Shibui's Stories daily during Tom's December dates is the only way to catch one. Contact: Yuichi Shibui (MMA founder and director), Instagram @shibuinsta_mania https://www.instagram.com/shibuinsta_mania/ ; brand Instagram @mountainmartialarts https://www.instagram.com/mountainmartialarts/ (Guerrilla Runs are announced only in these accounts' Instagram Stories, which vanish after a day) ; web store https://store.mountainmartialarts.tokyo/

items.title: Shopping at Pilgrim Surf+Supply Shibuya, a grown-up shop for the city-and-nature dual life (【お買い物動画】都会と自然のデュアルライフ！！洗練されたファッション、サーフ、アウトドアが全て詰まった"ピルグリム サーフ+サプライ"で大人のお買い物！！)
items.detail: Pilgrim Surf+Supply Shibuya, run in Japan by BEAMS under Chris Gentile's New York direction, is one of the only shops in Tokyo that mixes surf gear with real clothing around a "city and nature dual life" idea, so it is a natural place to show a surf or sun bandana. Why: Pilgrim is one hop from Shingo Arai through BEAMS, and this tour shows what it stocks, how staff talk about product and which Tokyo surf people (Yuya Ofuji, the Ambient Wetsuits riders) gather around it. Tom can walk in, see where a bandana would sit on the shelf and ask staff in person. Contact: Pilgrim Surf+Supply Tokyo (BEAMS), 1F 1-14-7 Jinnan, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo, tel 03-5459-1690, open 11:00-20:00, https://pilgrimsurfsupply.jp/ ; Instagram @pilgrimsurfsupply_japan_news https://www.instagram.com/pilgrimsurfsupply_japan_news/ (product questions go to the store by phone). Host Yuya Ofuji (OVY director, Ambient Wetsuits co-founder): Instagram @yuyaofuji https://www.instagram.com/yuyaofuji/

items.title: Staying Fluid with Chris Gentile (Pilgrim Surf + Supply)
items.detail: Pilgrim's founder says the person who wins people over is "the 25-year-old asking a million questions with a smile," so Tom should walk into Pilgrim Tokyo curious and in person, not with a hard pitch. Why: Pilgrim mixes surf hard goods with clothing from small makers, its Tokyo shop is run by BEAMS (the same company as Setinn's Shingo Arai), and Chris calls Japanese retailers the best in the world, so a surf or sun bandana is a natural thing for Tom to show there. Contact: Pilgrim Surf+Supply Tokyo (run by BEAMS), 1F 1-14-7 Jinnan, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo, tel 03-5459-1690, 11:00-20:00, https://pilgrimsurfsupply.jp/ ; Japan Instagram @pilgrimsurfsupply_japan_news https://www.instagram.com/pilgrimsurfsupply_japan_news/ (its bio says product questions go to the store by phone); Chris Gentile through the New York shop, Instagram @pilgrimsurfsupply https://www.instagram.com/pilgrimsurfsupply/ (33 Grand St, Brooklyn)

items.title: "Big boys need big clothes": Sillage's loose-fit philosophy (「Big boys need big clothes.」大男孩的寬鬆主義－Sillage)
items.detail: Sillage's own site runs What We Wear, a store for small brands and artists' work, so offering Tom's bandanas for it is a more natural ask than requesting a meeting. Why: This is a fan's secondhand explainer, but it gives Tom the basics on Nicolas Yuthanan Chalmeau (Paris-raised, in Tokyo since 2017, oversized comfort, "customize your own clothes"). Sillage now has a physical store in Daikanyama, which Tom can visit. items.title: How traditional Japanese hand-dyed towels are made
items.detail: Todaya Shoten in Ningyocho will make a fully custom chusen-dyed tenugui for anyone who orders enough, but bold shapes and 7 or 8 colours at most dye best, and fine detail gets lost. Why: This is the end-to-end process Tom would go through to have his bandana print made as Tokyo tenugui (stencil in Mie, chusen dyeing in Edogawa, finishing in Ningyocho), so he can walk in knowing the steps, the design limits and the questions to ask. items.title: Gotta Hand it to Kamawanu! Shopping for Traditional Hand Towels in Tokyo
items.detail: Kamawanu's Harajuku shop, in the basement of the Ota Memorial Museum, shows how far a tenugui brand can push one standard 35 x 90 cm cloth with seasonal motifs, playful modern prints and licensed collaborations. Why: It is in Harajuku near the Setinn flagship and is the clearest example in Tokyo of a modern tenugui brand Tom can study for sizing, folding, display and price, and Kamawanu also takes original tenugui orders. items.title: Double-sided dyeing with the traditional Tokyo Honzome (chusen) technique, Tokyo Wasarashi (Katsushika) (6 伝統的な染技法"東京本染(注染)"による「両面染色技術」[ 東京和晒株式会社（葛飾区）])
items.detail: Tokyo Wasarashi (now Tokyo Wasen) is a 1889 chusen dye works in Katsushika that runs hands-on tenugui dyeing classes with professional tools and was openly asking to collaborate with designers. Why: It is the most accessible way for Tom to touch Tokyo chusen dyeing during a two-week trip (book a class and leave with a real Tokyo-dyed sample), and a factory that has said it wants designer partners is a natural place to raise a small bandana run. Contact: Tokyo Wasen (東京和染, formerly Tokyo Wasarashi; name change notice dated 2026-10-01), 4-14-9 Tateishi, Katsushika-ku, Tokyo, tel 03-3693-3334 (weekdays 9:00-18:00), https://tenugui.co.jp/ ; IG @tokyowasen https://www.instagram.com/tokyowasen/ ; dyeing workshop booking https://souzou-kan.info/koubou/offer/ (GO TOKYO lists a 120-minute short course at 6,600 yen for 2 to 6 people)
